texts: mixed: the report itself is clean - Pell as the teller, Coraline Ash as the addressee, and the reported "sky-cats molt while they hunt" becomes a usable per-sky-cat rule with the molting held inside the hunting. The weak point is the date: "day 68 of Year 1" lands as a day-number plus a year, and a day number is read as a day of a MONTH, so a day-of-year count cannot be ordered against the other episodes' dates. If your calendar has months, date it with one: "On day 8 of the third month of Year 1, Pell told Coraline Ash that sky-cats molt while they hunt." (substituting the real month and day-of-month).
good. "molting sky-cats" reads as an adjectival restriction, so the reported claim becomes a fireable rule - any sky-cat that is molting drops feathers - with teller and addressee both covered.

mixed: the writing and the notebook are covered, but "a thin sky-cat year" with a verbal predicate is read as ONE particular thin year bringing ONE particular harvest, so the standing rule you are stating is not recoverable and will not connect to any later thin year. Put it in the bare plural so it becomes a rule: "Coraline Ash wrote in the notebook that thin sky-cat years bring thin feather harvests."

mixed: the telling and the "keeps the Stilllight Lantern lit" state (continuation included) all land, but "always" leaves no trace whatever - a reported clause carries no strength channel for a frequency adverb, and "the village" is one specific individual rather than a kind, so no quantifier record is licensed either; the result is indistinguishable from a plain "the village keeps the lantern lit". Give the frequency a stated period, which does survive: "Old Vesh told Pell that the village keeps the Stilllight Lantern lit every night." (use "every day and every night" if you mean round the clock).
